q: Match the following germ-cell milestones with the time they occur — 1) Spermatogenesis first begins 2) Oogenesis first begins 3) Primordial germ cells reach the genital ridge … A) Puberty B) Intrauterine life C) 5th-6th week of gestation
exp: Spermatogenesis starts only at puberty, oogenesis starts in intrauterine life, and PGCs migrate to the genital ridge by the 5th-6th week.

q: Fill up: A full cycle of spermatogenesis takes ______ days, of which the morphogenetic phase of spermiogenesis alone occupies ______ days.
exp: Spermatogenesis takes 70-74 days (~72 days) and spermiogenesis alone takes 10-14 days.

q: Which of the following statements about human spermatozoa is TRUE?
opts: Sperm acquire progressive motility only during epididymal transit, not in the testis
Sperm gain the ability to fertilise an oocyte while still inside the seminiferous tubules
Ejaculated sperm are immediately capable of fertilising an oocyte without further change
Spermatozoa normally remain motile in the female genital tract for barely two to three hours
exp: Motility is acquired during epididymal transit; fertilising capacity requires capacitation in the female tract, and sperm survive there for days.

q: Match the germ-cell population with its number — 1) Oogonia at 20 weeks' gestation 2) Oocytes at birth 3) Oocytes at puberty … A) ~7 million B) 1-2 million C) 300,000-400,000
exp: Peak oogonial number is ~7 million at 20 weeks, falling to 1-2 million at birth and 300,000-400,000 by puberty.

q: Fill up: A teratoma shows tissue from all three embryonic layers, so its cell of origin behaves as a ______ cell, whereas a normal primordial germ cell is only ______.
exp: Teratomas reveal the totipotent potential of germ cells, while normal PGCs are bipotent — able to form spermatogonia or oogonia only.

q: A 32-year-old woman's oocytes fail to fertilise in vitro until albumin is added to the culture medium; albumin acts as a sterol acceptor and strips cholesterol from the sperm membrane. Which step was being reproduced?
opts: Capacitation — removal of cholesterol and seminal glycoproteins from the sperm membrane
Acrosome reaction — release of acrosin and hyaluronidase from the acrosomal cap
Cortical reaction — enzyme release that hardens the zona pellucida around the oocyte
Spermiation — detachment of mature spermatozoa from recesses in the Sertoli cell
exp: Capacitation is cholesterol and glycoprotein removal from the sperm membrane (reproduced in vitro by albumin), and it must precede the acrosome reaction.

q: Fill up: Fertilisation normally occurs in the ______ of the fallopian tube and the zygote reaches the uterine cavity about ______ days later.
exp: Fertilisation occurs in the ampulla and the conceptus takes roughly 3-4 days of tubal transport to reach the uterine cavity.

q: Match the implantation landmark with its post-ovulation timing — 1) Blastocyst enters the uterine cavity 2) Blastocyst attaches to the endometrium 3) Implantation is completed … A) Day 3-4 B) Day 6-7 C) Day 11-12
exp: The blastocyst enters the cavity on day 3-4, attaches on day 6-7 and implantation is complete by day 11-12.

q: Which of the following statements about trophoblast differentiation is TRUE?
opts: Syncytiotrophoblast is the outer multinucleated layer that secretes hCG and invades the endometrium
Cytotrophoblast is the outer multinucleated layer and is the main source of hCG secretion
Syncytiotrophoblast forms by fusion of decidual stromal cells around the implanting blastocyst
Cytotrophoblast alone erodes maternal sinusoids, since it is the invasive layer in the first trimester
exp: Cytotrophoblast is the inner mononuclear stem layer; syncytiotrophoblast is outer, multinucleated, hCG-secreting and invasive.

q: All of the following are derived from the inner cell mass EXCEPT:
exp: The trophoblast (and hence syncytiotrophoblast) comes from the outer cell mass; the embryo, amnion and yolk sac come from the inner cell mass.

q: Fill up: Preimplantation genetic testing is performed on a biopsy of the ______ taken on day ______ of development.
exp: Blastocyst-stage trophectoderm biopsy on day 5-6 is standard, because sampling the inner cell mass would risk the embryo itself.

q: A woman at 8 weeks of gestation has an abdominal CT scan; the calculated fetal dose is 4 rad (40 mGy). She asks whether the pregnancy must be terminated. What is the most appropriate counselling?
opts: Termination is not indicated — doses below 5 rad show no measurable rise in malformation or loss
Termination is advised — any exposure above 1 rad after 6 weeks causes microcephaly
Termination is advised — 4 rad lies above the 2 rad threshold for organogenic damage
Termination is not indicated — before 10 weeks radiation can only cause growth restriction
exp: Below 5 rad there is no detectable increase in malformation, growth restriction or loss, so termination is not medically indicated.

sec: Teratogenic drugs: category X & specific malformations
q: Match the drug with its classic fetal effect — 1) Warfarin 2) Sodium valproate 3) Lithium … A) Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve B) Nasal hypoplasia with stippled epiphyses C) Lumbosacral neural tube defect
exp: Warfarin causes nasal hypoplasia and chondrodysplasia punctata, valproate causes neural tube defects, and lithium causes Ebstein anomaly.

q: All of the following are recognised features of congenital cytomegalovirus infection EXCEPT:
exp: PDA and pulmonary stenosis belong to congenital rubella; CMV gives periventricular calcification, chorioretinitis and sensorineural deafness.

q: Fill up: At term the placenta weighs about ______ g, which is roughly ______ of the fetal weight.
exp: The term placenta weighs about 500 g and its ratio to the fetus is about 1:6.

q: Which of the following statements about trophoblastic invasion of the spiral arteries is TRUE?
opts: Extravillous trophoblast replaces the musculoelastic media of spiral arteries by 20-24 weeks
Endovascular trophoblast invasion stops at the decidua and never reaches the myometrial segment
Spiral arteries keep their smooth muscle throughout pregnancy, so intervillous flow stays pulsatile
Cytotrophoblast plugs persist until the third trimester and only dissolve after 28 weeks
exp: The second wave of trophoblast invasion converts spiral arteries into low-resistance flaccid tubes by 20-24 weeks; plugs disappear by 10-12 weeks.

q: Fill up: The term placenta contains about ______ cotyledons, and each is supplied by a single ______ artery.
exp: There are roughly 15-20 cotyledons, each supplied by one truncal (stem villous) artery arising from the chorionic plate vessels.

q: A 29-year-old at 6 weeks of gestation has a corpus luteum removed at laparotomy for a large haemorrhagic cyst. If no hormonal support is given, what is the most likely outcome?
opts: Pregnancy loss, because the luteo-placental shift is not complete until 8-10 weeks
Normal continuation, because hCG alone maintains the decidua from the fourth week onward
Normal continuation, because the fetal adrenal axis takes over progesterone synthesis immediately
Preterm labour at 32 weeks, since progesterone is what suppresses myometrial contractility
exp: Before the luteo-placental shift at 8-10 weeks the corpus luteum is the sole source of progesterone, so its removal without support causes loss.

q: Match the following about placental steroidogenesis — 1) Substrate the placenta takes from the mother 2) Enzyme pair the placenta lacks 3) Principal estrogen of pregnancy … A) 17-alpha-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase B) Maternal LDL cholesterol C) Estriol
exp: The placenta uses maternal LDL cholesterol, lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase, and makes estriol from fetal DHEA-S and 16-alpha-OH-DHEA-S.

q: Which of the following statements about human chorionic gonadotropin is TRUE?
opts: The beta subunit is hCG-specific and is what assays measure; the alpha subunit is shared with TSH, LH and FSH
Serum hCG keeps rising through the second trimester and peaks only at around 28 weeks
A doubling time slower than seven days is entirely normal between 4 and 8 weeks of gestation
hCG first appears in maternal blood only after implantation is complete at about day 14
exp: hCG peaks at 8-10 weeks and then falls; the beta subunit is assay-specific, and hCG is detectable from about day 8-9, well before day 14.

q: All of the following predispose to placenta accreta spectrum EXCEPT:
opts: Grand multiparity without any uterine surgery
Previous caesarean section with an anterior low-lying placenta
Previous endometrial curettage or Asherman syndrome
exp: Accreta spectrum needs a deficient decidua from endometrial damage — scar, curettage, previa or myomectomy; parity alone does not scar the myometrium.

sec: Cord insertion anomalies, vasa previa & Apt test
q: At 38 weeks, membranes rupture spontaneously and are immediately followed by fresh vaginal bleeding and fetal bradycardia. Vaginal blood is mixed with water; after adding alkali the supernatant stays pink. What is the diagnosis and the immediate step?
opts: Vasa previa with fetal haemorrhage — immediate caesarean section
Placental abruption with maternal bleeding — stabilise and aim for vaginal delivery
Bloody show from cervical dilatation — reassure and await spontaneous labour
Uterine rupture — laparotomy and repair of the uterine scar
exp: A positive Apt test (alkali-resistant fetal haemoglobin turning the supernatant pink) means the blood is fetal — vasa previa demands immediate caesarean.

q: Fill up: Fetal erythropoiesis begins in the ______, and the predominant haemoglobin at term is ______.
exp: The mesoblastic (yolk-sac) phase starts first, and HbF still predominates at term, with HbA rising only after birth.

q: Match the amniotic fluid colour with its usual meaning — 1) Golden yellow 2) Green 3) Port-wine or red-brown … A) Meconium staining B) Rh isoimmunisation with bilirubin C) Old blood, as in abruptio placentae
exp: Golden fluid means bilirubin from haemolysis, green means meconium, and port-wine or red-brown means old intrauterine bleeding.

q: A 34-year-old at 37 weeks has an amniotic fluid index of 4.2 cm with a single deepest vertical pocket of 3.1 cm. How should this scan be reported, and what follows?
opts: Oligohydramnios by AFI, though the deepest pocket is still adequate — look for rupture and monitor
Normal study, because both the AFI and the deepest vertical pocket are within normal limits
Polyhydramnios, because the AFI is above the 95th centile for gestational age
Severe oligohydramnios by both criteria, so immediate caesarean delivery is indicated
exp: AFI at or below 5 cm is oligohydramnios, while a deepest pocket of 3.1 cm is still above the 2 cm threshold — the two methods disagree and must both be reported.

q: All of the following are causes of polyhydramnios EXCEPT:
exp: Renal agenesis removes fetal urine output and causes oligohydramnios; obstruction, impaired swallowing and fetal polyuria cause polyhydramnios.

q: Which of the following statements about oligohydramnios is TRUE?
opts: Potter sequence follows prolonged severe oligohydramnios beginning before about 22-24 weeks
Amniotic band syndrome is caused by oligohydramnios and is prevented by amnioinfusion
An amniotic fluid index of 8 cm is diagnostic of oligohydramnios in the third trimester
Isolated oligohydramnios at term is by itself an indication for immediate caesarean delivery
exp: Only early, severe, prolonged oligohydramnios causes pulmonary hypoplasia with Potter facies and limb deformities; bands are a separate amnion-rupture problem.

q: Fill up: In severe polyhydramnios, amnioreduction removes fluid at about ______ mL per hour, and the drug used to reduce fetal urine output is ______.
exp: Slow decompression at about 500 mL/hour limits abruption and preterm labour, and indomethacin reduces fetal urine output (with ductal constriction as the caveat).
